title: China and its economic model
subtitle: 1978-2024: a miracle under control
subject: comprendreLeMonde
description: In forty years, China has gone from an isolated agricultural country to the second largest economic power in the world.

hero.hook: An isolated agricultural country that became the second world power in a single generation.

blocks.text: In the space of four decades, **China** has achieved an economic transformation without parallel in history, going from an isolated agricultural country to the second largest economic power in the world. This shift was made possible by the gradual abandonment of the strictly communist model, in favor of an original mix between political control and entrepreneurial dynamism.
This spectacular success is now reaching a turning point: aging of the population, massive debts and international tensions threaten the continuation of this story.

The breaking point was in 1978, when  took over the country after the death of Mao Zedong. Convinced that isolation leads to an impasse, he launched a policy of “reform and opening”: agricultural land regained freer management, and **special economic zones** were created on the coast, of which Shenzhen became the symbol. **[[Deng Xiaoping]]**

blocks.caption: Shenzhen, a simple fishing village in the 1970s, has become a technological megalopolis in just a few decades.

blocks.text: These areas attract foreign investors thanks to an abundant and inexpensive workforce. Between 1978 and 2018, China maintained average growth of 9.5% per year, an exceptional pace which enabled more than 800 million people to escape extreme poverty in forty years.
By the end of the 1970s, China's GDP was equivalent to that of Spain. Today, it is around ten times higher than that of Japan, its neighbor.

This economic miracle has nothing to do with limitless liberalism. The state retained exclusive control over land ownership and strategic sectors, using growth as a source of legitimacy for the . This is called “state capitalism”: a dynamic market economy for consumer goods, but tight control over energy, telecommunications and finance. **[[The Chinese Communist Party (CCP)]]**
At the same time, a powerful private sector has developed, driven by technology companies like Alibaba, Tencent and Huawei, today capable of competing with the American giants of Silicon Valley.

sections.title: New Silk Roads and internal faultlines

blocks.text: China's rise is also expressed through infrastructure. Launched in 2013 by , the Belt and Road Initiative (“new Silk Roads”) is one of the largest investment projects in modern history: ports, railways and pipelines financed by Beijing across Asia, Africa and Europe, to secure its supplies and expand its influence. **[[Xi Jinping]]**
China's high-speed rail network alone accounts for more than two-thirds of the total length of high-speed lines in operation worldwide.

This external power, however, hides internal fragilities. Chinese growth has relied heavily on real estate and infrastructure, which has created considerable debt. The near-bankruptcy of real estate giant Evergrande in 2021 revealed the flaws of a market boosted by speculation, even as Chinese growth is now slowing to around 5% per year.

sections.title: The price of aging and tensions with the West

blocks.text: The most formidable challenge for China's future is not economic, but demographic. The one-child policy, imposed between 1980 and 2015, slowed births for decades. China's population began to decline in 2022, reducing the number of workers and increasing costs for the healthcare and pension systems.

Added to this are growing tensions with the West, in particular around the status of  and access to semiconductors, these electronic chips essential to all modern industry. To reduce its dependence on the outside world, Beijing is now seeking to strengthen its technological self-sufficiency. **[[Taiwan]]**

In forty years, China has lifted 800 million people out of poverty thanks to a model combining Party control and entrepreneurial dynamism. It is now facing a structural slowdown, linked to the aging of its population, massive debt and major geopolitical tensions.
